Prevention: Moko disease are likely to be effective against blood disease:
Avoid moving infested plant materials to a disease-free area.
During sanitation procedures, disinfect implements and cutting tools with household bleach (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) before and after pruning each plant.
Disinfect shoes with bleach before leaving an infested area.
Clean clothes worn in the field.
Avoid damaging the plants when transplanting.
Destroy plant debris, by composting away from uninfected plants.
Do not replant in infested fields or move or plant infested material in other farms.
The disease is thought to be transmitted by insects from infected male and possibly female flowers; remove the male bud as soon as the last female fingers emerge.
The bud is best removed by twisting off using the hand or a forked stick.
Monitoring: Symptoms may depend on host variety, route of infection and growth stage.
In mature leaves, transient yellowing, followed by a loss of vigour, desiccation and necrosis.
In mature plants, the base of the petiole collapses causing dead leaves to hang down around the plant stem.
Young leaves stop emerging and may turn white/yellow before drying.
Vascular tissue shows a reddish-brown discoloration that may extend throughout the plant or may be confined to the central fruit stem.
Cut stems or peduncles may exude bacterial ooze that is cream to reddish-brown to black.
May cause blackening and shrivelling of male flowers and peduncles.
Fruits may appear unaffected, but show a reddish-brown discoloration internally and become dry or rotted.
Symptoms are similar to those produced by
Panama disease of banana (does not cause internal fruit discoloration, premature fruit ripening and bacterial ooze).
Direct Control: Destroy any infected plants and all infected material from the plantation by cutting and composting or burning.
